paragraphs.text: The clinical news was led by gene editing and muscular dystrophy. Beam Therapeutics said its base-edited sickle cell therapy, risto-cel, met its goal in a Phase 1/2 study, cutting the most painful complications of the disease over a full year, according to BioPharma Dive, Endpoints and Fierce. Beam says it could file with the FDA as soon as year-end. Fierce frames it as setting up a contest with Casgevy and Lyfgenia, the two existing one-time sickle cell therapies. PepGen's stock more than doubled after Phase 2 data in myotonic dystrophy type 1. Fierce says the results hit analysts' best-case scenario, and BioPharma Dive says they compare favorably with RNA-based drugs in testing at Novartis and Dyne. The data come from a small study, so the read-across should be treated cautiously. ImmunityBio moved the other way. It reported a pivotal Phase 3 win for Anktiva in front-line non-muscle invasive bladder cancer, but the stock fell about 20% because detailed data were missing and third-quarter financials disappointed.

paragraphs.text: Mirum met the primary endpoint in a second late-stage trial of brelovitug in hepatitis D and plans an FDA submission, though Endpoints notes it will face growing competition. J&J scored a second Phase 3 win for Caplyta in bipolar mania and is preparing a label expansion. Merck KGaA won an FDA nod in a rare tumor disorder, which Fierce says sets up a showdown with Ono and Daiichi. On the safety side, the FDA is ordering a rare eye risk, the so-called eye stroke, added to the warnings on a dozen GLP-1 drugs, including Ozempic and Zepbound. The effect on sales is unclear from the reports, but it is a labeling overhang for the most heavily traded theme in pharma.

paragraphs.text: On deals and financing, AstraZeneca bought its partner Omniose for bacterial vaccine bioconjugation technology, with no price in the headlines. Oura agreed to pay $625 million in cash for Counsel Health, an AI primary-care startup. STAT notes Oura recently delayed its own IPO plans. In provider M&A, HealthSpan Partners, the Bon Secours affiliate, raised its offer for Surgery Partners to $6 billion after a rival bid, adding $300 million. London's Oyster Therapeutics raised a $60 million Series A-2 for tau-degrading pills. Venture financing is still flowing even as layoffs continue. Vertex cut 78 jobs at the San Diego biotech it bought for $10 billion, Coherus is cutting 30% of staff, and Capricor and NextCure disclosed layoffs ahead of an approval decision and a merger respectively. Summit also lost commercial leaders before the FDA decision on ivonescimab.

paragraphs.text: Policy risk is rising after the midterms. Congressional Democrats sent requests to every drugmaker with a most-favored-nation pricing deal, asking for unredacted agreements, and incoming committee chairs are moving toward an investigation, per STAT and Endpoints. The White House is still pushing Heidi Overton's FDA nomination through the short lame-duck window. A WSJ analysis finds the international pricing policy has not yet lowered new-drug prices in the US, though 27% fewer drugs have launched in Europe. Fierce reports experts worry the Treasury's COINS Act proposal on China biotech investment is ambiguous about joint ventures. Separately, a court win helped WuXi AppTec largely escape the Pentagon's Chinese military company list. STAT also reports that members of the USPSTF preventive care panel hold ethics waivers despite owning pharma stocks and private practices.

paragraphs.text: For providers and payers, hospitals are bracing for Medicaid work requirements and deep funding cuts from January 1, per the NYT. The administration announced $10 billion in second-year Rural Health Transformation awards. Kaiser Permanente grew third-quarter revenue 9% to $34.7 billion and doubled its operating margin, though its bottom line fell short of last year's. Fierce says insurers cited positive Medicaid and open-enrollment trends even as medical cost trend stays a pressure point. The WSJ notes hospital stocks are 'feeling blue in a good way', but the list gives no detail. Hims & Hers posted $890.4 million in revenue and a $33 million net loss while tightening its outlook.

paragraphs.text: Inflation dominates the macro picture. The Labor Department said October consumer prices rose 0.4%, above expectations. The NYT describes a broadening of price pressures, and the WSJ calls it a third straight month of firm underlying inflation. The 10-year Treasury yield moved above 5% on Tuesday, helped by hawkish Fed commentary. Governor Waller said he is leaning toward a December hike and could back a half-point move depending on data. Another official, Paulson, a voter, expects more tightening but prefers a gradual pace. Goldman Sachs now pencils in additional Fed tightening. Treasury futures are pointing to further weakness, and the WSJ argues one more hike looks like the beginning rather than the end. The big unknown is the size of the December move. One dollar strategist cited by the WSJ says further gains need stronger pricing of a 50 basis point hike.

paragraphs.text: Currencies reflect it. The dollar hit a four-week high, and the yen slid to two-month lows against it. Gold was higher, and Julius Baer called the long-term outlook compelling, expecting US inflationary pressure to ease next year so the Fed can be less aggressive than feared. Elsewhere, central banks are tightening too. Bank of England deputy governor Lombardelli signaled another rise is likely soon unless inflation weakens, and the NIESR think tank wants the rate raised to around 5%. The Bank of Canada minutes show it hiked to guard against upside inflation risk despite slack. Japanese savers are buying retail government bonds at a record pace as yields reach 2.39%.

paragraphs.text: Equity futures rose on a tech rebound. CoreWeave beat on third-quarter revenue and announced about $9 billion of planned prepayments, which MarketWatch says eased debt worries. The WSJ is more guarded, saying the company found a workaround to capital constraints for now but its plans still need capital-market cooperation. The results lifted Nasdaq futures and European chip stocks, and the FT says US tech is set to extend its rebound with Anthropic's IPO also supporting sentiment. An FT piece reports investors are questioning AI energy start-ups, whose shares keep sliding while they spend heavily. The WSJ separately flags OpenAI's mounting losses, with no detail given. Nvidia is the exception: its shares fell as the affair involving Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy deepened, DealBook says analysts are asking about succession, and the Commerce Department delayed adding connected company Megaspeed to its entity list.

paragraphs.text: Energy is mixed. Oil rebounded after a two-day drop as uncertainty over US-Iran talks persisted, and the FT says it had fallen below $90 as Trump pulled back from a strike threat. US gasoline fell below $4 for the first time since July, while the NYT says heating costs will rise 7% this winter, with heating oil users facing about 70% increases because the Iran war cut supply. European gas rose back above €85 per megawatt-hour on faster storage withdrawals.

Vestas fell after missing some revenue estimates. Nissan returned to a loss and cut its sales view on weakness in China. Spain had its first general strike in 14 years over housing costs ahead of a November 29 snap election. Zimbabwe is seeking MSCI Frontier Markets inclusion for its dollar-only exchange, and Turkey widened its fund-manipulation crackdown with the arrest of the former Takasbank CEO. paragraphs.text: Funding costs are the main theme. An FT Markets piece says the era of cheap money is ending for corporate America, with rising borrowing costs hurting some companies more than others. The 10-year above 5% makes that point sharper. The NY Fed data show households still meeting monthly debt payments on autos, student loans and mortgages, a steady backdrop for consumer credit. Children's Place shows the corporate side. MarketWatch says it is filing for bankruptcy with $881 million of debt, citing falling birth rates, cautious consumers and competition.

paragraphs.text: Private credit coverage is mostly about what happens when borrowers struggle. Pinsent Masons warns professional services firms face rising legal risk from private credit failures, and Paperjam says the real test begins when borrowers struggle. In Australia, Law360 reports the sector launched guidelines under ASIC scrutiny, while Kalkine asks whether listed property manager Centuria is exposed to the crackdown. Money is still being raised. Saudi Venture Capital invested in Jadwa Investment's flagship private credit fund, and Alternative Credit Investor looks at Standard Life's pension risk transfer partnership and private credit focus. These are mostly trade pieces with limited detail, but together they show the asset class moving from fundraising to scrutiny.

paragraphs.text: In public markets, Lannebo's sustainable corporate bond fund fell 0.2% in October as wider credit spreads weighed. That is a small data point but it fits the rate-driven repricing. The FT says the global sell-off during the Iran war has pushed investors toward a new split in the eurozone bond market, with France and Belgium on the wrong side. China plans a $2 billion dollar-denominated sovereign bond sale in Hong Kong, extending a busy year of offshore fundraising. Yahoo Finance Australia has a piece on high-yield bond funds, which offers no new information.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's IPO dominates. The FT reports bankers are preparing to raise the valuation to $1.5 trillion or more on strong investor demand. CNBC, citing the FT, says the offering could be enlarged, and earlier reports pointed to a target of up to $1.4 trillion. Reuters, however, calls the IPO scaled back and says it is fueling AI uncertainty, which does not line up neatly with the FT's account. The headlines do not reconcile the two, so the structure and size are worth watching for clarification. The NYT says Nvidia planned to invest $10 billion alongside the offering, the largest of several new commitments from big companies. An FT opinion piece warns that shadow insider sales and circular supply-chain backing could cause after-market indigestion despite huge demand. Bloomberg says the deal arrives as investors worry about AI's outlook, and the FT's calculator frames fair value anywhere between $500 billion and $4 trillion. Morningstar asks which Canadian funds already hold the stock.

paragraphs.text: Regulation is bending other deals. Western Union ended its $500 million takeover of Intermex after pushback from California regulators. The UK competition regulator warned that McCormick's $65 billion Unilever foods tie-up could harm competition and gave the companies a week to respond. Cinven is exploring a sale of UK wealth manager True Potential, which Bloomberg says could add to a string of UK wealth deals. Alibaba said it filed confidentially in September to list its Nvidia-rival chip unit T-Head in Hong Kong. In Mexico, the FT profiles David Martínez's challenge to Carlos Slim through a joint-venture purchase of an AT&T business.
